title: HP and Asus shift some PC making back to China due to AI-driven cost hikes
content:
TAIPEI -- Leading PC makers, including HP of the U.S. and Asus and Acer of Taiwan, are combating soaring component costs by shifting some production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China and using a new generation of contract manufacturers.
HP and Asus are among PC makers returning some production to China after building facilities in Vietnam and Thailand as part of a "China+1" diversification strategy. (Illustration by Michael Tsang)
Emerging contract manufacturers reap benefits of supply-chain strategy reversal

report.summary: HP and Asus are shifting some PC production from Vietnam and Thailand back to China as AI-driven surges in memory and component costs squeeze hardware margins.
report.background: The PC industry spent years pursuing a "China+1" strategy, building assembly hubs in Vietnam, Thailand, India and Mexico after the 2018 US-China tariff war and the COVID-era supply shocks. China's share of notebook manufacturing fell steadily as brands chased tariff avoidance and geopolitical hedging. But the AI data-center boom has inverted that calculus: hyperscaler demand for HBM, DRAM and advanced packaging is absorbing memory and component capacity, pushing contract prices sharply higher and inflating PC bill-of-materials costs. At the same time, China retains the densest supplier clusters, shortest logistics loops and deepest pool of manufacturing talent. With margins thinning and buyers unwilling to absorb full cost increases, PC brands are re-routing volume to China and to a new cohort of aggressive Chinese contract manufacturers rather than paying premium component prices abroad.
key_points: AI capex is crowding out consumer electronics: data-center buildouts are consuming HBM and DRAM output, lifting memory and storage contract prices. For PC makers, a single component category can erase thin single-digit margins, forcing them to chase the cheapest possible assembly and logistics base rather than the most geopolitically fashionable one.

The shift is tactical, not a full reversal. HP and Asus are moving only some volume back, keeping Vietnam and Thailand plants running as a hedge against tariffs and policy risk. The "China+1" model is being downgraded from strategic doctrine to flexible option, with production allocated by cost per unit rather than by country.

A new generation of Chinese contract manufacturers is capturing the returning orders. These emerging ODMs undercut established Taiwanese and Southeast Asian suppliers on pricing and speed, aided by proximity to component clusters and less rigid cost structures, reshaping who builds the world's laptops.

China's ecosystem advantage has reasserted itself. Dense supplier clusters, faster component replenishment, mature engineering talent and lower inbound freight costs make China cheaper per unit again, particularly when component prices themselves are volatile and inventory buffers matter more than tariff lines.

Geopolitical risk remains unresolved. US tariffs on Chinese goods and export-control uncertainty still hang over the strategy, meaning any re-routing could reverse again if trade policy shifts or if memory prices normalize once new AI capacity comes online.
report.impact: The re-routing is a visible symptom of AI's gravitational pull on global manufacturing: consumer devices are now competing with data centers for memory and components, and losing on price. For the AI industry, it confirms the memory supercycle is real and broad, with allocation increasingly favoring hyperscalers. For developers, expect higher prices and slower availability for RAM, SSDs, GPUs and prebuilt workstations, and eventually upward pressure on cloud and inference costs as hardware economics pass through. For regular users, laptops and desktops may get more expensive or ship with weaker base specs as brands protect margins. Suppliers in Vietnam and Thailand face slower ramp-ups, while Chinese ODMs win back relevance.
report.tools: To follow the story, track memory and component pricing via TrendForce and DRAMeXchange, plus Counterpoint and Omdia for PC shipment and BOM data. For hands-on supply-chain modeling, ERPNext and Odoo Community are open-source ERPs with BOM, procurement and multi-plant cost modules; OpenBoxes handles inventory across sites. PCPartPicker and CamelCamelCamel give consumer-level price history to gauge how component inflation reaches retail, while Nikkei Asia's Tech Asia and DigiTimes cover contract-manufacturer shifts.
